comparison: Perfect overlap on claims C57-C60, C84 regarding independence of event number and timing effects. OpenEval finds the histogram matching analyses methodologically sound despite marginal significance, while peer reviewers note apparent inconsistencies between interval distributions and event rate differences across behavioral outcomes, requesting clarification.

High overlap on claims C5, C17, C49-C56, C83, C90-C91 regarding temporal relationships between beta events and perception. OpenEval supports the ~200ms window findings, while peer reviewers question the characterization of event timing patterns (noting doublets/triplets) and point out apparent inconsistencies in Figure 9 interval distributions.

High overlap on claims C4, C15-C16, C38-C41, C43-C44, C82 regarding event rate as primary predictor. OpenEval finds comprehensive statistical support across datasets, while peer reviewers explicitly request direct comparisons with conventional power analyses to validate whether event-based features truly provide superior prediction.

Substantial overlap on claims C18, C61-C67, C73, C81, C101 regarding bursty nature of beta events. OpenEval finds convergent evidence from multiple analyses supporting the bursty characterization, while peer reviewers express significant concern about distinguishing burst vs. dynamic amplitude accounts, requesting bimodality tests and phase-preservation analyses to avoid 'relabeling something we already know.'

High overlap on claims C103-C105, C107-C109 regarding spectral characteristics and other frequency bands. OpenEval treats these as contextual findings supported by citations, while peer reviewers explicitly request extension to alpha and gamma bands to establish frequency specificity, noting evidence that alpha also predicts somatosensory performance.

Both address claims C71-C72 regarding robustness to alternative event definitions. OpenEval finds the continuous supra-threshold region analysis supports robustness, while peer reviewers specifically question whether imposing minimum intervals between bursts or amplitude relaxation criteria would yield the same results.

Substantial overlap on claims C13-C14, C19, C21, C23, C25-C29 regarding negative relationship between prestimulus beta power and behavioral performance. OpenEval finds strong statistical support across datasets, while peer reviewers acknowledge this as established and do not challenge these basic power-behavior relationships.

Both address claims C74-C77 regarding competing hypotheses about beta generation mechanisms. OpenEval finds Figure 12 analysis clearly supports the Bursty Generator hypothesis, while peer reviewers' broader concerns about distinguishing burst vs. dynamic amplitude accounts suggest uncertainty about this mechanistic interpretation.

Partial overlap on claims C3, C31-C32 regarding transient nature of beta oscillations. OpenEval finds Figure 2 data directly supportive, while peer reviewers express concern that 'epochs with prominent (and largely sustained) beta oscillations may be wrongfully classified as epochs with high burst rate' due to noise effects.

Partial overlap on claims C35-C37 regarding stereotyped event characteristics. OpenEval finds event characteristics well-documented in Figure 5, while peer reviewers request critical information about trial inclusion proportions and whether analyses include all trials or only those with events, stating this is essential to assess predictive importance.

Both address claims C45-C46 regarding cutoff-dependent relationships. OpenEval finds sliding cutoff analyses provide nuance to main results, while peer reviewers' general concern about distinguishing event-based from conventional approaches suggests these findings require further validation.

Partial overlap on claims C20, C22, C24 regarding behavioral performance relationships. OpenEval finds statistical support for these relationships, while peer reviewers request clarification about MEG source locations and LFP recording sites, stating this is 'essential for constraining the study's conclusions.'

Partial overlap on claims C33-C34 regarding event definition methodology. OpenEval finds the 6X median cutoff justified by correlation analysis, while peer reviewers request direct comparisons with conventional power estimates to validate superiority of event-based analyses.

Partial overlap on claims C78-C79 regarding cross-species consistency. OpenEval emphasizes this strengthens generalizability, while peer reviewers acknowledge the cross-species approach but do not specifically challenge these consistency claims.

Minimal overlap on claim C100 regarding distinct mechanisms at different power levels. OpenEval finds support from multiple analyses despite lack of clear bimodality, while peer reviewers' request for additional comparisons suggests uncertainty about this interpretation.

Minimal overlap on claims C49-C50. OpenEval supports temporal relationship findings, while peer reviewers question how zero-event trials were handled in threshold derivation and correlation analyses, requesting clarification about trial inclusion criteria.
Minimal overlap on claim C42. OpenEval supports event rate as primary predictor, while peer reviewers question trial inclusion and threshold derivation procedures that may affect these findings.

Minimal overlap on claims C47-C48 regarding optimal criteria. OpenEval finds support from optimal criterion analysis, while peer reviewers question whether correlation strength would differ when including zero-event trials and using different correlation methods.

Minimal overlap on claims C68-C69 regarding event characteristics. OpenEval supports bursty process characterization, while peer reviewers request information about trial inclusion proportions to assess how representative these characteristics are.

Minimal overlap on claim C70. OpenEval finds support for bursty characteristics, while peer reviewers question whether alternative event definitions (minimum intervals, amplitude relaxation) would yield same results.
Minimal overlap on claim C30 regarding motor readiness control. OpenEval finds this rules out motor confounds, while peer reviewers accept this control analysis without challenge.
